pattern.crimePattern: curio middleman kills the beadwork co-op treasurer whose direct export deal cut out his five-fold markup, and leaves her in a dry river bed
pattern.notes: Fictional co-op, middleman, exporter and bead colour. Middlemen underpaying beadwork groups is a real grievance; no real business or group is depicted. The Mvua flyer is a deliberate decoy in the WHY bank.

ob.text: A boda rider reports a woman's body in the dry bed of the Talek river below the bridge at 06:30. She is identified as Nashipae Kores (44), treasurer of the Enkiteng Women's Beadwork Group.

facts.text: Nashipae Kores was found dead in the dry bed of the Talek river below the bridge at 06:30.
One head wound. No marks of a struggle in the sand around her.
Loose glass seed beads in her hair and clothing folds, many of them a deep turquoise.
No signs of a struggle in the sand; pickup tyre tracks run down the bank and back up.
Her bag lies beside her with KSh 6,200 inside, untouched.
In her bag: a signed direct export contract with a fair-trade buyer, at five times Gitonga's price.
In her bag: a printout of a Nairobi exporter's catalogue, the co-op's designs at KSh 1,500 each, "sourced through Murithi Curios". Gitonga pays KSh 300.
Co-op store: one jar missing from the turquoise row; the floor swept, but beads in the cracks; a shard of thick glass under the table.
Minutes: the Saturday meeting ended at 19:30. "Nashipae to stay and pack the export order." Seenoi had argued about payment shares.
Minutes: the payment-share quarrel was voted on and settled at that meeting.
Receipt book: Murithi Curios' last order was paid in full on 2 February.
Nasieku: "Enkiteng blue is ours alone. We import that batch. Nobody in Talek has it but us."
Nasieku: the bead stock tallies, every jar, except the one that's missing.
Nasieku went home to her family after the meeting.
Co-op notice board: "Landowners! Advance payments on your conservancy lease — cash today. Mvua Holdings. Till 880 214."
Records, Gitonga's line: Talek mast 19:00–21:40, then the Narok road from 22:00.
Murithi Curios till book: sales at 19:55, 20:20, 20:40, 21:00, 21:20 and 21:35, each initialled by Elvis.
Nkoile: Seenoi was home at the manyatta from 19:45, milking and cooking.
Moseka: he found her at 06:30 crossing the bridge. The boda stage register has him at the stage from 18:00 to 06:15.
Gitonga's pickup: deep turquoise beads in the ridges of the load bed; its tyre tread matches the tracks on the river bank.
Autopsy: a heavy blow from a smooth, curved glass object. Fine glass fragments in the wound.
Autopsy: no injuries from a fall onto sand, and no marks of strangling.
Autopsy: death between 20:00 and 21:30.
Lab: the glass in the wound and the shard under the co-op table are the same thick bead-jar glass.
Gitonga: "I closed my shop at seven and drove to Narok."
Gitonga: "I've supported those women for ten years."
Gitonga admits he went to the co-op store on Saturday evening "to talk to her".
Gitonga: "Business is business. I left her packing."
Elvis: "Boss left for Narok at seven."
Elvis: the boss left for Narok at ten. He came back from the co-op at about nine and swept out his pickup, and told Elvis what to say.
Seenoi: "I was home."
Nasieku: "We trusted him. We had nobody else to sell to."

interrogations.intro: Gitonga meets you at his shop door, hand on his heart. "Nashipae! Ten years I have bought their work. I closed at seven and drove to Narok."

topics.reply: That is the market. I take the risk; I carry the stock. They could not reach Nairobi without me.

interrogations.intro: Elvis keeps folding the same shuka on the counter. "Boss left for Narok at seven."
Seenoi bounces the baby on her back and doesn't sit. "I was home."

topics.reply: We argued, yes. Then we voted, and I lost, and that was the end of it. Ask my mother-in-law where I was.

interrogations.intro: Nasieku stands among the jars, turning one in her hands. "This colour. Look at this colour."

topics.reply: We trusted him. We had nobody else to sell to.

interrogations.intro: Moseka sits on his motorbike at the bridge. "I saw her from the bridge at half past six. I called the post."

contradictions.reaction: "He left at ten. He came back from the co-op at nine, sweeping his pickup. He told me what to say."
His hand comes off his heart. "...I went to talk to her. Business is business. I left her packing."
Gitonga looks at the turquoise beads in the evidence bag. "Three hundred shillings," he says quietly. "That was a fair price in this town." Then nothing.

timeOfDeath.note: From the autopsy; Gitonga was at the store from about 20:25 and back at his shop by about 21:00.

proof.concludes: She was struck with a bead jar inside the co-op store, among the Enkiteng blue beads that exist nowhere else in Talek. The river bed is only where she was left: no struggle, no fall injuries, tyre tracks.
Her direct export contract was about to cut Gitonga out of a five-fold markup.
Gitonga was in Talek until 21:40, not on the road at seven; he went to the store, and was back sweeping his pickup by nine. She died between 20:00 and 21:30.

His pickup made the tracks into the river bed, and Enkiteng blue beads are in its load bed. At the co-op store, Gitonga Murithi struck Nashipae with a glass bead jar because her direct export deal was cutting him out.

eliminations.why: No struggle in the sand, no fall injuries, and tyre tracks down the bank.
The glass and the beads come from the co-op store.
She stayed at the store to pack, and the glass in the wound is the store's.
The beads and glass on her come from the co-op store.
Elvis rang up sales every twenty minutes at the shop from 19:55 to 21:35.
Seenoi was home at the manyatta from 19:45.
Nasieku went home to her family after the meeting.
Moseka was at the boda stage all night by its register, and found her at dawn.
No fall injuries; glass in the wound.
Her bag and its cash were untouched.
That quarrel was Seenoi's, voted on and settled.
The stock tallies except the broken jar.
A flyer on the wall for everyone; nothing in her bag or his books ties it to either of them.

reconstruction.text: For ten years Gitonga pays the co-op KSh 300 a piece and sells the same pieces to a Nairobi exporter for KSh 1,500.
In January Nashipae finds the exporter's catalogue online and signs a direct contract with a fair-trade buyer, at five times his price.
Saturday, 19:30. The meeting ends; she stays to pack the first export order. At about 20:30 Gitonga comes to make her cancel. She refuses.
He strikes her with a heavy glass jar of Enkiteng blue beads. It breaks; beads scatter across the floor.
He drives her 400 m to the bridge and leaves her in the dry river bed, sweeps the floor badly, and tells Elvis to say he left for Narok at seven. At 22:00 his phone is on the Narok road.

clockPlan.note: Records on Gitonga's line, then a warrant on his pickup. The glass match takes 8 h. Every site is on foot in Talek.
